title: Hazard Spotting
blurb: How to spot hazards before they cause harm, fix what you safely can and report the rest.
siteNotes: How to report a hazard you cannot fix, and who to tell on each shift (your manager will show you).
How to take faulty equipment out of use here (tag, sign, or unplug and tell a manager).
Known hazard areas in each department.

cards.title: Hazard Spotting
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- say what a hazard is and give examples
- look for hazards as you move through your area
- deal with it or report it, never walk past

cards.title: Anything that could cause harm
cards.body: A hazard is simply anything with the potential to cause harm. Once you start looking, they are everywhere. Hazard spotting is training your eyes to notice them before they cause an accident, not after.

cards.title: Up, down and around
cards.body:
Look up, down and around as you move through your area, rather than switching onto autopilot.

A great habit is to ask yourself: if a guest walked through here right now, what might hurt them? You know your own work area better than anyone, so you are the best-placed person to spot when something is not right.

cards.title: Spotting is only half the job
cards.body:
The other half is doing something about it.

- If you can deal with it safely and quickly, do so: mop the spill, coil the cable, move the box.
- If you cannot fix it safely yourself, such as a faulty appliance or damaged flooring, take it out of use if you can and report it.

right.title: Take out of use and report

cards.title: That someone is you
cards.body: The one thing you must never do is walk past a hazard thinking someone else will sort it out. It takes moments to make something safe or to flag it, and it could save a colleague or guest from a serious injury.

items.title: Report it early
items.text: This is how we stop accidents before they happen.

items.title: Fix it if you safely can
items.text: Mop it, coil it, move it.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm
- Look up, down and around, and ask what might hurt a guest
- If you can deal with it safely and quickly, do so
- If you cannot, take it out of use if you can and report it
- Never walk past a hazard: that someone is you

options: An accident that has already happened
Anything with the potential to cause harm
Any item left out of its place
A fault written in the log
cards.why: A hazard is simply anything with the potential to cause harm.

cards.q: A blocked fire exit is a serious hazard.
cards.why: A blocked fire exit is one of the examples of a hazard in the training.

cards.q: As you move around, you should look...
cards.why: Look up, down and around rather than switching onto autopilot.

cards.q: You're often the best-placed person to spot a hazard in your own work area.
cards.why: You know your own work area better than anyone, so you are best placed to spot when something is not right.

cards.q: What's a good question to ask yourself when checking for hazards?
options: Is this actually my job to fix?
What might hurt a guest right now?
Is a manager around to ask?
cards.why: Asking what might hurt a guest walking through trains your eyes to notice hazards.

cards.q: You find a faulty appliance you can't fix. What should you do?
options: Take it out of use if you can, and report it
Keep using it as carefully as you can
Leave it for the next shift to find
Switch it off at the wall and forget it
cards.why: If you cannot fix it safely, take it out of use if you can and report it.

cards.q: 'Someone else will sort it out' is a good attitude to hazards.
cards.why: That someone is you. Never walk past a hazard.

cards.q: You spot a small spill you can safely clean. You should...
cards.why: If you can deal with it safely and quickly, do so: mop the spill, coil the cable, move the box.

cards.q: Reporting hazards early helps prevent accidents.
cards.why: Reporting hazards early is how we stop accidents before they ever happen.

cards.q: Which one of these is a common workplace hazard?
cards.why: The training lists spills, trailing cables, wobbly shelves, blocked fire exits, frayed plugs and chemicals left out.
